blueprint_findings.title: Industrial and Manufacturing Strength
blueprint_findings.body: Affordable infrastructure, an experienced aerospace labor base, and physical room to scale. Three things California and Florida no longer offer at the same price point.
blueprint_findings.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, "Where Arizona has a real advantage"

blueprint_findings.title: Missing Identity and Narrative
blueprint_findings.body: Arizona is still perceived nationally as a supporting player rather than a leader. The gap is positioning. The gap can close.
blueprint_findings.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, "Where Arizona is falling short"

blueprint_findings.title: Capital Formation Gaps
blueprint_findings.body: Venture and growth capital flowing into AZ space remains a fraction of what flows into California, Texas, or Florida. AZ-founded companies routinely have to leave the state to raise.
blueprint_findings.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, "Where Arizona is falling short"

blueprint_findings.title: Talent Pipeline at Scale
blueprint_findings.body: Arizona State University and the University of Arizona produce thousands of high-skill graduates per year across engineering, science, and mission systems. Most leave the state within five years of graduation.
blueprint_findings.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, "Where Arizona has a real advantage"

blueprint_findings.title: Legal and Policy Friction
blueprint_findings.body: Regulatory uncertainty around export controls and commercialization pathways adds drag on deal flow that competing states have already reduced.
blueprint_findings.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, "Where Arizona is falling short"

blueprint_findings.title: Cross-Sector Convergence
blueprint_findings.body: Arizona sits at the intersection of commercial space, national security, academia, and advanced manufacturing. No other state holds all four corners at once.
blueprint_findings.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, "Where Arizona has a real advantage"

blueprint_findings.title: Strategic Geography and Stability
blueprint_findings.body: Minimal natural-disaster risk and strong logistics positioning make Arizona reliable for operations, testing, and mission continuity. Insurance costs and downtime risk are meaningfully lower than competing space states.
blueprint_findings.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, "Where Arizona has a real advantage"

blueprint_findings.title: Lack of Operational Infrastructure
blueprint_findings.body: Arizona builds missions but does not operate them locally. The work moves to Colorado, Maryland, and California. The talent follows.
blueprint_findings.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, "Where Arizona is falling short"

blueprint_findings.title: Fragmentation Across the Ecosystem
blueprint_findings.body: Universities, companies, government, and the military all hold AZ-based assets that should be operating as one system. They are not yet connected.
blueprint_findings.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, "Where Arizona is falling short"

blueprint_milestones.description: Translation into a working ecosystem strategy.

blueprint_priorities.summary: Infrastructure across the full operational lifecycle, not launch alone: research and development, design and integration, manufacturing and testing, orbital access, data systems and commercial operations. The Blueprint's finding is that Arizona already holds these assets and that integrating them, rather than creating new ones, is the work.
blueprint_priorities.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, Phase II - Infrastructure (Findings 01-03)
blueprint_priorities.blurb: Infrastructure across the full operational lifecycle, not launch alone. Arizona already holds the assets; integration is the work.

blueprint_priorities.summary: Launch and orbital access as one layer of a statewide system. Two emerging Arizona spaceport initiatives are underway, Yuma holds launch potential and logistics, and Sierra Vista offers operational and reentry infrastructure. The Blueprint asks for these to be designed as complementary parts of one plan rather than separate projects competing for the same federal dollars.
blueprint_priorities.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, Phase II - Infrastructure (Findings 01, 04)
blueprint_priorities.blurb: Launch and orbital access as one statewide system: two emerging spaceport initiatives, Yuma logistics, Sierra Vista reentry.

blueprint_priorities.summary: The human layer of the space economy, which the Blueprint calls the new bottleneck. Arizona already hosts established companies across life support, mission systems and avionics, and its universities run active NASA missions and space-biology research. The constraint is the on-ramp: the state produces high-skill graduates and then loses most of them within five years.
blueprint_priorities.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, Phase II - Human Frontiers (Findings 01-03)
blueprint_priorities.blurb: The human layer, and the Blueprint's named bottleneck. Arizona produces the graduates and then loses most of them.

blueprint_priorities.summary: Commercialization as the primary growth engine. The orbital economy is projected to grow from roughly $630 billion in 2023 to $1.8 trillion by 2035, but leadership positions are set well before the market reaches full scale. The Blueprint's named gap is capital formation: Arizona-founded companies routinely have to leave the state to raise.
blueprint_priorities.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, Phase I - Information; Phase II - Technology Finding 04; Gap -05/05
blueprint_priorities.blurb: Commercialization as the growth engine, against a capital-formation gap that pushes AZ-founded companies out of state.

blueprint_priorities.summary: Operating missions from Arizona, not just building them. The Blueprint names this as the state's first gap: Arizona builds missions but does not operate them locally, so the work moves to Colorado, Maryland and California, and the talent follows. Data systems and downstream services are the layer where that changes.
blueprint_priorities.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, Gap -01/05 and Phase II - Infrastructure Finding 01
blueprint_priorities.blurb: Operating missions from Arizona, not just building them. Today that work moves to other states, and the talent follows.

blueprint_priorities.summary: National security space, where Arizona is already strongest. The state ranks first nationally in the concentration of guided missile and space vehicle manufacturing employment, $3.5B in SDA Tranche 3 Tracking Layer contracts were awarded in 2025, and Davis-Monthan and Yuma Proving Ground are named as candidate integrated nodes for cleared space-systems testing.
blueprint_priorities.source_note: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026, At a Glance; Phase III - Defense lane
blueprint_priorities.blurb: National security space, where Arizona is already strongest: first nationally in space manufacturing employment.

congress_events.name: Arizona Space Congress
congress_events.description: The annual working convening, where representatives of the space economy meet to debate and rank the sector's priorities. Discussion is captured and synthesized by AI in real time, validated by the participants so a human stays in the loop, and then voted into a shared roadmap, the Space Blueprint.
congress_events.summary: Leaders from industry, government, academia and investment convene to rank Arizona's space-economy priorities and vote them into the Arizona Space Blueprint.

directory_companies.name: The Space Nurse, LLC
directory_companies.description: Space Nurse, LLC integrates clinical nursing expertise into commercial spaceflight through Human Systems Integration and clinical auditing. Currently, the launch industry relies on bespoke, manual physician reviews that are unscalable and inconsistently applied across varying flight architectures. To solve this, we are seeking accelerator support to build our flagship tech-enabled service: the Medical Reconciliation Hub. Once developed, this platform will utilize rules-based Go/No-Go clinical logic to ingest, reconcile, and validate passenger health data against specific aerospace mission profiles. To build and validate the prototype rapidly, we will leverage synthetic data models. This strategy allows us to safely test our clinical decision support algorithms without the immediate regulatory friction of handling real protected health information. Because this complex triage requires human clinical judgment, the software is designed to be managed by our own highly trained personnel. To scale this workforce, we are establishing the Clinical Bioastronautics Professional credential to train nurses and allied health practitioners to operate the hub. By pairing specialized clinical operators with our proprietary software, we transform medical clearance from an unpredictable bottleneck into a repeatable, high-integrity workflow.

directory_listings.title: Stratospheric Ballooning: Arizona's Quiet Space Advantage
directory_listings.description: World View and Near Space Corporation are pioneering a new category of space access from Arizona's high desert.
directory_listings.body:
## Why Arizona for Stratospheric Access?

The answer is simple: weather and geography. Arizona's high desert offers over 330 clear days per year, low humidity, minimal air traffic conflicts over vast swaths of the Sonoran Desert, and proximity to both US military test ranges and civilian research institutions.

World View Enterprises operates from Tucson's Spaceport, launching balloons to 100,000+ feet with payloads ranging from scientific instruments to defense ISR platforms.

## The Market Is Expanding

Stratospheric ballooning isn't a niche — it's emerging as a cost-effective complement to satellite operations:

- **Persistent surveillance**: Balloons can loiter over an area for days or weeks at a fraction of satellite cost
- **Science platforms**: NASA and NOAA regularly contract for atmospheric research payloads
- **Defense applications**: The military's interest in high-altitude platforms has surged post-2022

## What's Next for Arizona

World View recently secured a $56M Series F. Near Space Corporation is expanding its launch cadence. Arizona's spaceport infrastructure and regulatory environment position the state as the default home for this sector.

directory_listings.title: Honeywell’s $500 Million Deal Is the Latest Proof Point in Arizona’s Defense and Aerospace Surge
directory_listings.description: Honeywell’s new $500 million production deal is the latest sign that Arizona is rapidly becoming a national hub for defense and aerospace manufacturing. As major firms and next-generation suppliers expand across the Phoenix-Mesa corridor, the state is emerging as one of the most strategic growth markets in America’s defense industrial base.
directory_listings.body:
Honeywell Aerospace’s new $500 million production agreement is more than a headline about one company expanding output. It is the clearest new signal that Arizona has moved into the front rank of U.S. defense and aerospace growth markets. Honeywell said the agreement will support a multi-year investment to expand production of navigation systems, missile steering and actuation technologies, and electronic-warfare products. Reuters reported the deal as part of a broader federal push to accelerate defense manufacturing capacity, while Arizona’s Family brought the story home by highlighting the practical effect for the state: more production of the systems that sit inside modern aircraft, missile platforms, and battlefield protection technologies.

That matters because Honeywell is not expanding into a vacuum. It is scaling inside a state that has spent the last several years turning aerospace and defense into one of its defining industrial strengths. The Arizona Commerce Authority says Arizona has attracted more than 60 aerospace and defense expansions over the past five years, representing more than $2.8 billion in investment and more than 12,500 projected jobs. That kind of number tells a bigger story than a single contract ever could: Arizona is not simply hosting aerospace companies; it is building a self-reinforcing industrial base.

In Greater Phoenix, the scale is already substantial. The Greater Phoenix Economic Council says the region’s aerospace and defense sector now employs more than 66,000 people, a figure that has grown by nearly 12% since 2018. The sector contributes billions to regional output and continues to expand as manufacturers, suppliers, and specialized service firms cluster around the same labor pool, infrastructure, and customer base. That density is important. Defense manufacturing does not thrive on isolated announcements. It thrives where supply chains, engineering talent, airport access, testing capacity, and procurement relationships begin to compound. Arizona is reaching that stage.

Honeywell’s announcement fits that pattern almost perfectly. The products named in the agreement are not generic industrial goods. They are high-value, mission-critical systems that depend on precision manufacturing, electronics integration, and a dependable network of upstream and downstream suppliers. When a company commits half a billion dollars to expand capacity in those areas, it usually means it sees not just demand, but confidence in the surrounding ecosystem. Arizona increasingly offers that confidence: a large technical workforce, available industrial land, military relevance, and faster logistics than many legacy aerospace hubs can now provide.

What makes the current moment especially significant is that the state is attracting both legacy anchors and newer-generation manufacturers at the same time. In January, Hadrian opened its Factory 3 facility in Mesa, a $200 million, 290,000-square-foot manufacturing and software hub expected to bring more than 350 jobs. GPEC described the site as part of Hadrian’s push to manufacture next-generation aerospace and defense technology with AI-enabled production methods. That is exactly the kind of capacity national defense planners have been trying to encourage: faster, more modern, more scalable supplier infrastructure closer to major customers and program demand.

Mesa, in particular, is emerging as one of the most important submarkets in the region. The city markets a 35-square-mile aerotropolis around Phoenix-Mesa Gateway Airport and highlights one of the country’s strongest aerospace and defense clusters, with major players and aviation-related employers concentrated around the airport corridor. Mesa Gateway itself says it hosts more than 40 companies and contributes $1.8 billion annually to the Arizona economy, while the surrounding district continues to attract aerospace, aviation, and defense tenants. That concentration matters because cluster economics are real: once enough specialized employers gather in one place, they make it easier for the next supplier, the next training provider, and the next advanced manufacturer to justify coming too.

The names arriving in that corridor show the breadth of the boom. Virgin Galactic has completed its Arizona spaceship manufacturing facility in Mesa, reinforcing the region’s appeal for advanced aerospace assembly and long-cycle engineering programs. FlightSafety International has also announced a new 100,000-square-foot learning center in Mesa, a reminder that serious aerospace growth is never just about factories. It also requires pilot training, maintenance instruction, simulation, certification, and workforce development. When production and training investment rise together, it is usually a sign of a maturing ecosystem rather than a short-lived wave.

This is why Honeywell’s expansion deserves to be read as a market signal, not merely a contract story. Arizona is becoming a place where defense suppliers can grow near primes, near specialized labor, and near logistics infrastructure that serves both domestic and cross-border operations. The state has already become one of the nation’s most active destinations for industrial investment more broadly. The Arizona Commerce Authority said in February that Arizona led the country from 2020 to 2025 in announced international investment, with more than $195.7 billion during that period. Aerospace and defense are benefiting from the same larger forces that are reshaping the state’s economy: speed to market, infrastructure, room to expand, and a business climate oriented toward advanced manufacturing.

There is also a national-security logic behind Arizona’s rise. The defense industrial base is under pressure to produce more, faster, and with greater resilience. That means Washington needs more than prime contractors with strong brands; it needs places where second-tier and third-tier suppliers can scale quickly and reliably. Honeywell’s new agreement points directly at that need. So does Hadrian’s Mesa facility. So does the steady buildout around Gateway. Arizona is increasingly valuable because it can support both the headline company and the supplier web underneath it.

For business leaders, investors, and policymakers, the takeaway is straightforward. The center of gravity in U.S. aerospace and defense is broadening, and Arizona is one of the clearest beneficiaries. Honeywell’s $500 million commitment did not create that trend. It confirmed it. The state is attracting capital, specialized manufacturing, workforce infrastructure, and industrial momentum at the same time. In that context, Honeywell’s move reads less like an isolated win and more like the latest evidence that Arizona has become one of America’s most important launchpads for the next era of defense and aerospace production.

As major firms and next-generation suppliers expand across the Phoenix-Mesa corridor, the state is emerging as one of the most strategic growth markets in America’s defense industrial base.

directory_listings.title: Arizona Semiconductor Workforce: 2026 Outlook
directory_listings.description: A look at hiring trends and talent pipelines for Arizona's growing semiconductor ecosystem.
directory_listings.body:
## The Talent Gap Is Real

Arizona's semiconductor industry is at an inflection point. TSMC's North Phoenix fab, Intel's Ocotillo expansion, and a dozen smaller suppliers are all hiring simultaneously — but the pipeline isn't keeping up.

ASU, Maricopa Community Colleges, and the Mesa Community College Semiconductor Academy are responding with accelerated programs. But there's a 2-3 year lag between curriculum and fab-ready talent.

## What Companies Are Doing

**Intel** has partnered with ASU for on-the-job training programs that bring students directly into Chandler fab operations.

**TSMC Arizona** is importing process engineers from their Taiwan fabs while aggressively recruiting from US universities — particularly for roles that don't require clearances.

**Microchip Technology** has expanded its Phoenix-area internship program to 200+ spots annually.

## The Next 12 Months

Hiring will stay competitive. Expect salaries for process engineers to climb another 8-12% in 2026. Companies with strong relocation packages and training programs will win the talent wars.
directory_listings.excerpt: With TSMC ramping, Intel expanding, and CHIPS Act funding flowing, Arizona needs 10,000+ new semiconductor workers by 2027. Here's what companies are doing about it.

directory_people.bio_short: Brett Mecum serves as Chairman of the Arizona Space Commission, working to attract space companies, grow the state's aerospace workforce, and position Arizona as a national leader in the space economy.

Jim Cantrell is CEO of Tucson-based Phantom Space Corporation, building affordable small launch vehicles. A veteran space entrepreneur, he previously co-founded SpaceX and has spent decades working on commercial space access.

David Ariosto is a space and technology journalist who hosts the Open Space podcast, exploring Arizona's emerging space economy through conversations with founders, policymakers, and industry leaders building the ecosystem.

Dr. Lindy Elkins-Tanton is Director of the ASU School of Earth and Space Exploration and Principal Investigator of NASA's Psyche mission to a metal-rich asteroid. One of Arizona's most prominent space scientists and a champion for space exploration.

Governor Katie Hobbs relaunched the Arizona Space Commission in 2026 and has made growing Arizona's space economy a priority, citing the state's existing aerospace infrastructure, military bases, and research universities.
I'm a Creative Director, brand strategist, and entrepreneur focused on building experiences that create clarity, inspire action, and bring ambitious ideas to life.
directory_people.bio_long:
I'm a Creative Director, brand strategist, and entrepreneur focused on building experiences that create clarity, inspire action, and bring ambitious ideas to life. For more than 25 years, I've led creative work across branding, digital products, communications, photography, marketing, and visual storytelling. My work has evolved beyond designing individual assets into directing entire brand ecosystems—aligning strategy, messaging, user experience, and visual identity around a singular vision.

Today, as Co-Founder and Chief Brand Officer of Space Rising, I lead the creative direction behind a platform designed to organize and accelerate the commercial space economy. That means shaping everything from our brand and digital products to our events, publications, communications, and member experiences. Every touchpoint is an opportunity to create trust, simplify complexity, and strengthen the connections that move industries forward.

My philosophy is simple: great creative direction isn't about making things look beautiful—it's about making ideas unmistakably clear. The strongest brands create understanding before they create attention. They make people feel something before asking them to do something.

directory_people.bio_short: Strategic and creative leader with more than two decades of experience advancing innovative programming, cross-sector collaboration, and brand engagement in science, space, and education sectors. Adept at managing end-to-end operations including fundraising, marketing, events, design, and digital platforms. Known for translating bold ideas into operational success and championing programs that connect people, purpose, and progress in the global space economy.

directory_reports.title: FAA Site & Reentry Licensing
directory_reports.description: A technical reference on 14 CFR Parts 420 and 433: the federal review process and implications for prospective Arizona spaceport applicants.

directory_reports.title: Federal Opportunity Capture Strategy
directory_reports.description: Federal funding and contracting pathways shaping Arizona's space and satellite ecosystem, 2026-2029.

directory_reports.title: Market Intelligence Report
directory_reports.description: Arizona space technology, satellite launch, and federal funding. Strategic analysis for investors, policy advisors, and industry stakeholders.

directory_reports.title: S. 2888: The SPACEPORT Act
directory_reports.description: Provisions, status, and advocacy implications of the SPACEPORT Act (S. 2888) for Arizona's spaceport ambitions.

directory_reports.title: The Legislative Triad
directory_reports.description: A deep-dive analysis of the Space Infrastructure Act (H.R. 1154), the LAUNCH Act (H.R. 5602), and the New Space Age Act (H.R. 10320).

directory_reports.title: Arizona Space Blueprint 2026
directory_reports.description: Space Rising's strategic plan for Arizona's space economy - the definitive public blueprint presented at the 2026 Arizona Space Congress. Companies, capital, workforce, policy, and infrastructure in one 40-page report.

directory_reports.title: ESA Space Environment Report 2026
directory_reports.description: ESA’s annual assessment of the orbital environment, based on activity through the end of 2025. It tracks launch growth, constellations, debris, reentries, mitigation compliance and long-term orbital sustainability, including a new Space Environment Health Index.

directory_reports.title: Is It Strategically Useful for the U.S. To Pursue Any Norms or Treaties That May Limit Its Freedom of Action in Space?
directory_reports.description: A Center for Space Policy and Strategy debate paper presenting contrasting views on whether space norms and treaties can improve security and stability enough to justify constraints on national freedom of action. It focuses on the strategic tradeoffs decision-makers face when shaping international rules for space.

directory_reports.title: The Space Economy at a Glance 2026
directory_reports.description: OECD’s broad benchmark of the global space economy, covering public budgets, private investment, orbital activity, satellite-enabled services, industrial concentration and dependencies. It also examines the economic importance and sustainability challenges of increasingly space-reliant economies.

directory_reports.title: UK Space Strategy
directory_reports.description: The United Kingdom’s updated national strategy for using space to support economic growth, defense, resilience and national security. It sets government priorities for capabilities, investment, industry development and international partnerships through the end of the decade.

directory_reports.title: Main Trends & Challenges in the Space Sector — 5th Edition 2026
directory_reports.description: PwC’s global review of the commercial, technological, geopolitical and regulatory forces reshaping space. It covers satellite communications, Earth observation, navigation, launch, space safety and the beyond-Earth economy, including AI, direct-to-device services and in-space manufacturing.

directory_reports.title: Cislunar Crossroads: Why a Domain That Transports Its Own Disturbances Needs Polycentric Information Sharing
directory_reports.description: MITRE examines why the Earth-Moon environment creates traffic, disturbance and safety challenges unlike those in conventional Earth orbit. The paper argues for distributed information-sharing and governance mechanisms that can scale as cislunar activity increases.

directory_reports.title: What Will It Take to Build a Lunar Economy?
directory_reports.description: Deloitte analyzes the infrastructure, demand, capital and commercial models required to turn lunar activity into a functioning economy. It maps potential industries and scenarios for sustained lunar operations, including a high-growth pathway producing hundreds of billions of dollars in cumulative value by 2050.

directory_reports.title: Orbital and Suborbital Launch Sites of the World 2026
directory_reports.description: BryceTech’s global reference map of active and proposed orbital and suborbital launch sites. It provides a quick view of launch infrastructure, geographic distribution and the expansion of spaceport capacity around the world.

directory_reports.title: Q2 2026 Global Space Activity
directory_reports.description: BryceTech summarizes global orbital activity during the second quarter of 2026, including launches, spacecraft deployed and national/commercial shares. The report highlights continued constellation-driven volume and the dominant role of high-cadence launch systems.

directory_reports.title: FY 2027 Defense Space Budget: Dramatic and Targeted Growth
directory_reports.description: The Aerospace Corporation’s Center for Space Policy and Strategy analyzes the sharp increase in proposed U.S. defense-space spending for FY2027. It breaks down where growth is concentrated, including classified programs, missile warning/tracking, command and control, and related architectures.

directory_reports.title: Smallsats by the Numbers 2026
directory_reports.description: BryceTech’s data-driven review of the smallsat market over the last decade, including annual deployment volumes, operators, missions, launch vehicles and megaconstellation effects. It provides a compact statistical picture of one of the fastest-scaling parts of the space industry.

directory_reports.title: Constellating Compute: China’s Domestic Policy Towards Orbital Data Centre Leadership
directory_reports.description: ESPI examines China’s movement from orbital-data-center concepts toward implementation and the domestic policy environment supporting that shift. It assesses implications for compute infrastructure in space, strategic competition and European technological sovereignty.

directory_reports.title: Continental Ambitions, Uncertain Paths: The African Space Agency's Role Through 2040
directory_reports.description: The Aerospace Corporation examines the African Space Agency’s mandate and potential evolution through 2040. Using multiple scenarios, it explores how governance, technology, sovereignty and resource choices could influence Africa’s expanding civil, commercial and security space activities.

directory_reports.title: Seeds of Scale — UK Space Agency Accelerator Impact Report 2026
directory_reports.description: An impact assessment of the UK Space Agency Accelerator and the growth of companies supported through its programs. It focuses on capital raised, commercialization, company development and the effectiveness of public investment in scaling space startups.

directory_reports.title: Supply Chain Due Diligence in Space-Based Manufacturing and Lunar Resource Extraction: Building Sustainable & Resilient Cislunar Operations
directory_reports.description: An academic analysis of supply-chain risks and due-diligence requirements for in-space manufacturing and lunar resource extraction. It considers critical materials, launch dependence, robotics, AI, licensing and resilience across emerging cislunar supply chains.

directory_reports.title: UK Space Agency Annual Report and Accounts 2025–2026
directory_reports.description: The UK Space Agency’s annual report combines agency performance and financial reporting with an overview of programs supporting the national space sector. It provides useful indicators on industry development, investment priorities, missions and institutional activity.

directory_reports.title: ESA Report on the Space Economy 2026
directory_reports.description: ESA’s annual economic analysis of the European and global space sectors, covering public funding, private investment, upstream and downstream markets, industrial competitiveness and security-related spending. It is one of the main current reference reports for Europe’s commercial space economy.

directory_reports.title: Development and Technology Trends for the Satellite Component of IMT Towards 2030 and Beyond
directory_reports.description: An ITU-R technical report on the evolution of satellite components within international mobile telecommunications through 2030 and beyond. It addresses technologies and architectures relevant to integrating satellite and terrestrial mobile connectivity.

directory_reports.title: Aeronautics and Space Report of the President: Fiscal Year 2025 Activities
directory_reports.description: NASA’s congressionally mandated annual compilation of U.S. government aeronautics and space activities across federal departments and agencies. It is a useful source for programs, policy activity, budgets and government-wide space initiatives.

directory_reports.title: Super Heavy Lift Launch: Unlocking the Future of Space
directory_reports.description: The Aerospace Corporation evaluates how super-heavy-lift launch could change space economics by lowering constraints on mass, volume and deployment scale. It examines market demand, utilization, launch cadence, megaconstellations and the commercial conditions required for sustainable economics.

directory_reports.title: The Sovereign Threshold: From Autonomous Access to Responsive Space
directory_reports.description: ESPI explores the shift from simply maintaining sovereign launch access toward responsive, resilient space capabilities. It looks at rapid reconstitution, launch, data-sharing and in-orbit operations and compares Europe’s trajectory with other major space powers.

directory_reports.title: The Case for Space Sustainability in 2026
directory_reports.description: Secure World Foundation provides a current primer on orbital congestion, debris and why sustainability has become an economic and operational necessity. It reviews the risks to space infrastructure and the policy and industry mechanisms available to reduce them.

directory_reports.title: Q1 2026 Global Space Activity
directory_reports.description: BryceTech’s first-quarter snapshot of global launches and spacecraft deployment in 2026. It tracks launch-provider and national shares, spacecraft counts and the continuing influence of large commercial constellations on overall activity.

directory_reports.title: Defining Factory in Space: Comparative Analysis of Components, Features, and Functions
directory_reports.description: A research paper proposing a structured definition of the emerging 'factory in space' concept. It compares manufacturing, assembly, servicing, maintenance, logistics and enabling technologies to clarify how an in-space industrial ecosystem could develop.

directory_reports.title: Alternative Diplomacy Pathways Amid the Crisis of Global Multilateral Fora
directory_reports.description: ESPI assesses how space diplomacy and governance are evolving as traditional multilateral institutions struggle to keep pace with rapid technological and geopolitical change. It examines regional, minilateral and other polycentric approaches to rules and cooperation.

directory_reports.title: EU Space Market Report
directory_reports.description: EUSPA’s market report analyzes commercial demand and technology trends across satellite navigation, Earth observation, secure satellite communications and space situational awareness. It connects space capabilities with downstream applications, revenues, user needs and market forecasts.

directory_reports.title: State of the Canadian Space Sector Report 2025
directory_reports.description: The Canadian Space Agency’s annual survey-based assessment of the national space sector. It covers revenue, GDP contribution, employment, exports, R&D and the economic performance of more than 200 organizations active in Canada’s space ecosystem.

directory_reports.title: State of the Satellite Industry Report 2026
directory_reports.description: The Satellite Industry Association’s annual industry benchmark, produced by BryceTech, covering satellite services, manufacturing, launch and ground equipment. It tracks global commercial satellite revenues, deployment trends and the industry’s role within the wider space economy.

directory_reports.title: State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology 2026
directory_reports.description: NASA’s Small Spacecraft Systems Virtual Institute compiles current publicly available small-spacecraft technologies and capabilities. Topics include spacecraft platforms, propulsion, power, avionics, communications, guidance, launch and mission operations.

directory_reports.title: Space Venture 2025
directory_reports.description: ESPI’s annual assessment of venture investment in the global space sector with particular attention to Europe. It examines funding volumes, deal patterns, investor types, geography and the increasing importance of defense and security-oriented companies.

directory_reports.title: Seraphim Space Index Q1 2026
directory_reports.description: Seraphim Space’s quarterly research tracks investment and public-market conditions across the global SpaceTech sector. The Q1 2026 edition provides a current view of capital flows, sector performance and investor sentiment around commercial space businesses.

directory_reports.title: Examples of Evaluating and Resolving Interference into RNSS Earth Stations from Multiple Spaceborne SAR Sensors in 1215–1300 MHz
directory_reports.description: An ITU-R technical study of spectrum-sharing and interference risks between radio-navigation satellite service ground stations and multiple spaceborne synthetic-aperture-radar systems. It provides practical evaluation methods for increasingly crowded space-frequency environments.

directory_reports.title: Artemis Rewritten: NASA’s New Moon Plan, Its Risks, and Whether the U.S. Can Still Beat China
directory_reports.description: CSIS analyzes changes to NASA’s Artemis architecture and schedule, including technical, programmatic and geopolitical implications. The paper examines the revised path to lunar operations and the risks surrounding U.S.-China competition at the Moon.

directory_reports.title: New Space, New Rules: Commercial Space Markets Are Taking Off
directory_reports.description: McKinsey examines the transition of several space markets from primarily government-funded activity toward commercial demand. It highlights where private-sector scale, new business models and cross-industry applications may create growth opportunities in the latter half of the decade.

directory_reports.title: Start-Up Space 2026
directory_reports.description: BryceTech’s annual review of investment in commercial space startups, covering financing totals, deal counts, company stages, geography and investor activity. The 2026 report captures the return of larger financings and changing capital-market conditions across SpaceTech.

directory_reports.title: 2026 Global Counterspace Capabilities Report
directory_reports.description: Secure World Foundation’s open-source assessment of counterspace programs and capabilities across major space powers. It compares co-orbital, direct-ascent, electronic warfare, directed-energy and cyber capabilities that affect the risk and resilience profile of the space economy.

directory_reports.title: Orbital Launches Year in Review 2025
directory_reports.description: BryceTech’s statistical review of worldwide orbital launch activity during 2025. It summarizes launch counts, spacecraft deployed, leading nations and providers, and the continued growth of commercial constellations and small satellites.

directory_reports.title: From Moonshots to Markets: The $1.8 Trillion Space Economy
directory_reports.description: McKinsey reviews the evolution of space from a specialized aerospace market into a broader economic platform supporting communications, navigation, data and other industries. It discusses the operational and commercial capabilities needed to scale toward a projected $1.8 trillion global space economy by 2035.

directory_reports.title: "A Geopolitical Awakening": The European Union and Space
directory_reports.description: The Aerospace Corporation examines Europe’s changing space posture as the EU increases investment in strategic autonomy, defense and sovereign capabilities. It discusses governance, funding and the implications of a more security-oriented European space sector.

directory_reports.title: Q4 2025 Global Space Activity
directory_reports.description: BryceTech’s quarterly review captures record-setting launch and spacecraft activity at the end of 2025. It provides comparative data by country and operator and illustrates the continuing industrialization of high-cadence commercial launch and constellation deployment.

directory_reports.title: Where Sensing Makes Sense — Opportunities for Advancing Europe’s Priorities Through Earth Observation
directory_reports.description: ESPI maps how Earth-observation capabilities can support major European policy and economic priorities. Drawing on hundreds of policy documents and EO projects, it examines opportunities across energy, agriculture, security, climate, emergency response, insurance and digital systems.

directory_reports.title: China’s Space Activity 2025: Metrics of a Rising Power
directory_reports.description: BryceTech provides a data-centered overview of China’s space activity, including launches, spacecraft, launch sites, missions and industry development. It is a useful benchmark for measuring the scale and commercial expansion of China’s space ecosystem.

directory_reports.title: Measuring the Space Economy with Input-Output Linkages
directory_reports.description: An economic-methodology paper proposing a reproducible framework for measuring the U.S. space economy through national input-output accounts. It separates direct space activity from upstream supply-chain and downstream production linkages and helps quantify sector dependencies.

directory_reports.title: COSMOS — Space Is Scaling Up
directory_reports.description: KPMG’s commercial-space outlook describes 2025 as a transition toward space becoming a dual-use industrial platform. It highlights direct-to-device connectivity, orbital data centers, Earth observation for insurance and the integration of space-derived intelligence into enterprise systems.

directory_reports.title: Government Response to 'The Space Economy: Act Now or Lose Out'
directory_reports.description: The UK government’s formal response to the House of Lords report on the national space economy. It addresses competitiveness, sector growth, critical infrastructure, security and proposed government actions intended to strengthen the UK’s position in space.

directory_reports.title: One Word, Many Approaches: A Transatlantic Look at Commercial Space Procurement
directory_reports.description: ESPI and The Aerospace Corporation compare how the United States and Europe define and use 'commercial' space procurement. The report distinguishes procurement models by where government and industry carry requirements, investment and risk, helping explain divergent market-development approaches.

directory_reports.title: Clear Orbit, Secure Future: A Call to Action on Space Debris
directory_reports.description: The World Economic Forum and Centre for Space Futures examine the economic consequences of orbital debris and the business case for mitigation. The report models potential costs and advocates prevention, incentives, improved coordination and international action to protect orbital infrastructure.

directory_reports.title: A Field Guide on European Space Governance
directory_reports.description: ESPI provides a practical guide to the institutions and decision-making structures that shape European space policy. It explains the relationships among the EU, ESA, national governments and other actors and how responsibilities and funding are coordinated.

directory_reports.title: Revisiting National Space Transportation Policy: It’s Not Just Rockets Anymore
directory_reports.description: The Aerospace Corporation argues that U.S. space transportation policy must address a broader ecosystem than launch vehicles alone. It considers changing transportation capabilities and policy needs as commercial space expands beyond traditional launch-to-orbit services.

directory_reports.title: Countering Russian Escalation in Space
directory_reports.description: The Atlantic Council examines Russian counterspace escalation and policy options for strengthening deterrence and resilience. It considers military, diplomatic, commercial and acquisition responses to threats that could disrupt critical space infrastructure.

the-space-nurse-llc.name: The Space Nurse, LLC
the-space-nurse-llc.footer: SpaceOS is a platform of Space Rising. Building connections that advance the space economy.

connect.heading: CONNECT WITH THE SPACE NURSE, LLC

whatWeDo.body: Space Nurse, LLC integrates clinical nursing expertise into commercial spaceflight through Human Systems Integration and clinical auditing. Currently, the launch industry relies on bespoke, manual physician reviews that are unscalable and inconsistently applied across varying flight architectures. To solve this, we are seeking accelerator support to build our flagship tech-enabled service: the Medical Reconciliation Hub. Once developed, this platform will utilize rules-based Go/No-Go clinical logic to ingest, reconcile, and validate passenger health data against specific aerospace mission profiles. To build and validate the prototype rapidly, we will leverage synthetic data models. This strategy allows us to safely test our clinical decision support algorithms without the immediate regulatory friction of handling real protected health information. Because this complex triage requires human clinical judgment, the software is designed to be managed by our own highly trained personnel. To scale this workforce, we are establishing the Clinical Bioastronautics Professional credential to train nurses and allied health practitioners to operate the hub. By pairing specialized clinical operators with our proprietary software, we transform medical clearance from an unpredictable bottleneck into a repeatable, high-integrity workflow.

whatWeDo.body:
Alpha Metalcraft Group (AMG), a vertically integrated metal‑forming manufacturer supporting critical missile, propulsion, and aerospace programs across the defense industrial base. AMG brings more than 100 years of heritage across four U.S. sites (Bethel CT, Commack NY, Danbury CT, and Pacoima CA), with deep expertise in:

- Deep draw metal forming (exotic alloys, heavy‑gauge, tight‑tolerance geometries)
- CNC and manual metal spinning for complex near‑net shapes
- Electroforming for precision nickel and nickel‑cobalt structures
- Full machining, welding, and assembly capabilities

Our teams support mission‑critical applications including micro‑turbines, combustor liners, exhaust nozzles, domes, hemispheres, seeker cold‑shields, and other structural components. 

AMG’s value to procurement organizations is straightforward:
- Reliable U.S. manufacturing footprint with AS9100 and NADCAP certifications
- Ability to form complex shapes in materials such as Hastelloy, Inconel, Titanium, Tantalum, Nickel, and Stainless
- Short lead times supported by in‑house tooling, engineering, and NPI processes
- Proven performance with primes and Tier‑1 propulsion and missile integrators

connect.heading: CONNECT WITH COMMERCIAL REAL ESTATE GROUP OF TUCSON LLC

whatWeDo.body:
Tenant & User Representation for Southern Arizona's Aerospace & Defense Sector
Commercial Real Estate Group of Tucson represents tenants and buyers exclusively — we never work for landlords or sellers, so every recommendation serves one side of the table: yours.
For aerospace and defense contractors, subcontractors, and suppliers expanding or relocating in Southern Arizona, that distinction matters.
Our services include:

Site Selection — Identifying and evaluating industrial, flex, and R&D properties across Tucson's I-10 Corridor, southeast submarkets, and Pima County, matched to your operational, security, and clearance requirements
Financial & Cost Comparison Analysis — Side-by-side evaluation of competing sites and lease structures, so decisions are grounded in real numbers, not guesswork
Economic Incentive Coordination — Identifying and pursuing available state and local incentives, including Arizona's Qualified Facility Tax Credit, Foreign Trade Zone benefits, Pima County/City of Tucson incentive programs, and workforce/job-training grants relevant to defense and aerospace employers
Lease & Acquisition Negotiation — Structuring terms that protect your interests over the life of a multi-year government contract cycle

We bring 25+ years of local market knowledge to every engagement, along with a working understanding of how defense-sector operations actually function day to day.
Our Difference Is Your Advantage™

tim-2.bio: I'm a Creative Director, brand strategist, and entrepreneur focused on building experiences that create clarity, inspire action, and bring ambitious ideas to life.
tim-2.name: Tim

about.body:
I'm a Creative Director, brand strategist, and entrepreneur focused on building experiences that create clarity, inspire action, and bring ambitious ideas to life. For more than 25 years, I've led creative work across branding, digital products, communications, photography, marketing, and visual storytelling. My work has evolved beyond designing individual assets into directing entire brand ecosystems—aligning strategy, messaging, user experience, and visual identity around a singular vision.

Today, as Co-Founder and Chief Brand Officer of Space Rising, I lead the creative direction behind a platform designed to organize and accelerate the commercial space economy. That means shaping everything from our brand and digital products to our events, publications, communications, and member experiences. Every touchpoint is an opportunity to create trust, simplify complexity, and strengthen the connections that move industries forward.

My philosophy is simple: great creative direction isn't about making things look beautiful—it's about making ideas unmistakably clear. The strongest brands create understanding before they create attention. They make people feel something before asking them to do something.
